title: Contextualism
definition: In the contemporary sense, the same sentence can make different claims in different conversations. In older epistemology, it also named the view Greco calls flexible foundationalism.

title: Proposition
definition: The claim a sentence expresses, which can be true or false. “It’s raining” can express a claim about Davis or about Tokyo, depending on where it’s said.

title: Epistemology
definition: The branch of philosophy that asks what knowledge is, what gives us good reason to believe something, and how we can tell.

title: Epistemic justification
definition: Having good grounds for what you believe. A reliable forecast may justify expecting rain, even on a day when the forecast happens to be wrong.

title: Foundationalism
definition: Some beliefs have support without needing other beliefs as reasons. They can then give us reasons to hold further beliefs.

title: Coherentism
definition: Beliefs get their support from fitting into a mutually supporting system. Greco’s opening taxonomy represents this as a chain that loops back.

title: Flexible foundationalism
definition: Reasoning can start from beliefs that are taken as settled here. Change the conversation or inquiry, and a different belief can serve as the starting point.

title: Sensitive invariantism
definition: “Knows” keeps a fixed meaning. Whether someone counts as knowing can still depend on their situation, such as how much is at stake for them.

title: Relativism
definition: The same claim can count as true or false depending on the standards of the person assessing it.

title: Expressivism
definition: On this approach, calling a belief foundationally justified can voice a commitment to treating it as a starting point.

title: Epistemic internalism
definition: A family of views that ties justification to what is available from the believer’s own point of view or to their mental states.

title: Epistemic externalism
definition: Justification can depend on facts outside your perspective, such as whether the process that produced your belief is actually reliable.

title: Semantic paradox
definition: A puzzle about meaning or truth. If “This sentence is false” is true, what it says makes it false.

title: Skeptical paradox
definition: A puzzle in which plausible ideas about knowledge or reasons lead to the conclusion that we know or can justify far less than we ordinarily think.

title: The regress problem
definition: If every reason needs another reason behind it, where does justification come from? Can the chain stop, loop back, or go on forever?

title: Taxonomy
definition: A way to sort views. Here Greco sorts answers by what happens to a chain of reasons.

title: Skepticism
definition: In Greco’s taxonomy, skepticism says that none of our beliefs can be justified.

title: Infinitism
definition: Every reason has a further reason behind it. The chain goes on forever, with a new reason at every step.

title: Circular reasoning
definition: An argument comes back to a claim it already relied on. Imagine using A to support B, then using B as the reason to believe A.

title: Regress-stopper
definition: A reason that can support an answer without itself needing another reason in the reasoning at hand.

title: Foundational justification
definition: A belief is justified without drawing that justification from other beliefs. Feeling a toothache can give you grounds to believe you have one.

title: Cartesian foundationalism
definition: Descartes’s approach seeks foundations that can withstand every possible doubt. Greco’s dilemma is that too few beliefs meet such a demanding test.

title: Indubitable
definition: Impossible to doubt. Greco reserves “undoubted” for claims that are treated as settled in a particular inquiry.

title: Undoubted
definition: Treated as settled in the current inquiry. A memory can be undoubted in an everyday conversation and questioned in an investigation.

title: Incorrigible
definition: In this debate, a belief is incorrigible when having it is enough to guarantee that it is true.

title: Moderate foundationalism
definition: Experiences such as seeing a light can directly justify a belief even though the belief remains open to doubt or error.

title: Ad hoc
definition: Added to rescue a view from a problem, with little independent reason to accept it.

title: Justification as a social activity
definition: Giving and defending reasons is an activity we do with others. On Annis’s approach, a belief has the status of being justified when it can be defended in that practice.

title: Appropriate objector-group
definition: The people whose objections count, given the community’s standards in Annis’s theory. A foundational belief is one this group would let pass without challenge.

title: Epistemic norm
definition: A standard for what it is reasonable to believe or ask for evidence about. Greco asks whether a whole community can get such standards wrong.

title: Epistemic community
definition: The group whose shared standards shape which reasons or objections a person is expected to answer.

title: Subjectivism
definition: The view that a judgment depends on someone’s attitudes or the standards of their group. Greco worries this leaves too little room for a whole group to be mistaken.

title: Hinge
definition: An assumption held steady so you can investigate something else. Asking someone what color they see takes for granted that they understand your question.

title: Inquiry
definition: An attempt to answer an open question. It works by holding some background assumptions steady so you can investigate the question at hand.

title: Transcendental argument
definition: An argument that asks what must already be in place for something we do to be possible. Here, asking questions presupposes taking some things as settled.

title: Epistemic entitlement
definition: On Wright’s view, a rational permission to rely on certain background assumptions to get an inquiry started.

title: Quantifier order
definition: ∀∃ says each inquiry has some hinge of its own. ∃∀ says there is one hinge that works for every inquiry. Switching the order makes a stronger claim.

title: Knowledge is evidence (E = K)
definition: Williamson’s view that your evidence consists of what you know. What you already know can give you grounds for further beliefs.

title: Inference
definition: Drawing a conclusion from other things you believe. Seeing people in heavy coats can lead you to conclude that it’s cold outside.

title: Inference to the best explanation
definition: Choose the hypothesis that best explains what you observe. Wet streets make rain a natural guess, though sprinklers might explain them too.

title: Attribution
definition: Saying that someone has a status, such as knowledge. In “Justine knows the time,” the person making the claim is the attributor.

title: General foundations
definition: Harman’s view that every belief is foundational. Each can serve as a starting point in reasoning.

title: Sensitivism about belief
definition: Whether someone counts as believing something can depend on what they are doing or on the conversation they are in.

title: Truth-conducive factors
definition: Things that make a belief more likely to be right. A clear view makes it easier to tell what color a car is.

title: Practical stakes
definition: What you stand to lose or gain if you are wrong. Being sure a train runs matters more if missing it means missing a flight.

title: Conversational context
definition: What the people talking are taking for granted or treating as a live possibility. It can affect which doubts matter to a claim of knowledge.

title: Semantics
definition: The study of what words and sentences mean. Here the question is whether “knows” changes what a sentence says across conversations.

title: Felicity
definition: Whether a remark fits the situation. Saying “It must be cold” fits when you are drawing an inference from a clue.

title: Metaethics
definition: The study of what moral judgments mean and how they can be true. For example, what are we doing when we call something wrong?

title: Speaker-relativism
definition: On the simple view Greco describes, saying “That’s wrong” amounts to saying that I disapprove of it.

title: Problem of disagreement
definition: If two speakers are each describing their own standards, both might be right. How can their opposite verdicts still amount to a genuine disagreement?

title: Access internalism
definition: A view that justification must in some way be accessible to the person who has it. Greco examines a strong version that gives you grounds to believe you are justified.

title: The (Access) principle
definition: If you have good grounds to believe P, you also have good grounds to believe that you have good grounds for P.

title: Prima facie
definition: At first sight, before you consider further evidence or objections.

title: Higher-order claim
definition: A claim about your knowledge, belief, or grounds. “My evidence supports the claim that it’s raining” is about your evidence.

title: First-order claim
definition: A claim about the thing you’re investigating. “It’s raining” is about the weather itself.

title: Supervenience
definition: One set of facts fixes another. If two situations match on all the facts in the base, they must match on the dependent facts too.

title: Supervenience base
definition: The facts that fix an outcome. If Peter’s words fix what Justine is justified in believing about the party, those words are the base.

title: Local supervenience base
definition: The facts that fix what someone is justified in believing among the possibilities taken seriously here. Peter’s words can serve as the base while it’s settled that Justine heard him.

title: Global supervenience base
definition: Facts that fix justification across all relevant possibilities. Peter’s words alone fail this test because Justine might have misheard him or have good reason to distrust him.

title: Epistemic access
definition: Being in a position to know the relevant facts. Justine has access to what Peter said if she heard him clearly.

title: Mental state
definition: A condition of someone’s mind, such as having a visual experience, feeling pain, or believing that it is raining.

title: Introspection
definition: Paying attention to your own thoughts or experiences. You can notice that you feel a toothache by attending to how you feel.

title: A priori
definition: Knowable by reasoning without needing observations to settle it. Once you understand the terms, you can tell that every triangle has three sides.

title: Cognitive home
definition: A domain of facts whose truth or falsity you can always tell with enough attention. The traditional version is supposed to be rich enough to fix what you’re justified in believing.

title: Mobile cognitive home
definition: Greco’s name for a cognitive home that can move as doubts change. If Justine might have misheard Peter, his email could become the new accessible basis.

title: Background presupposition
definition: Something the reasoning takes for granted. In the party example, everyone starts by assuming Justine heard Peter.

title: Phenomenology
definition: Here, how an experience feels from the inside, such as what seeing a color looks like to you.

title: Antiluminosity
definition: The idea that even features of your own experience can be hard to know in borderline cases. As daylight fades, you may be unable to tell exactly when the room became dark.

title: Epistemic defeat
definition: New information cancels or undercuts the grounds you had for a belief. Peter’s reputation for pranks can undermine your reason to take his announcement at face value.

title: Outright belief
definition: Taking a claim to be true. You could instead spread your confidence between possibilities, such as giving 7:00 a 70% chance and 8:00 a 30% chance.

title: Chain of reasons
definition: A series of answers to “Why believe that?” You expect rain because of the forecast, and you trust the forecast because it uses recent weather data.

title: Contextual factors
definition: Features of the situation that may affect what counts as knowing or being justified. Greco’s examples include the stakes, the conversation, and the inquiry underway.

title: Linguistic data
definition: Evidence from how people use and understand language. For instance, do people withdraw “I know” when the conversation brings a new possibility into play?

title: Epistemic status
definition: A standing such as being justified, being known, or being justified without further reasons. The paper asks what makes attributions of those standings correct.

title: Possibilities taken seriously
definition: The alternative ways things could be that matter to the current inquiry. At first, everyone considers 7:00 and 8:00 while taking it for granted that Justine heard Peter.

title: Inter alia
definition: Among other things.

title: Mutatis mutandis
definition: The same reasoning applies after making the necessary changes. Here, swap 7:00 for 8:00.

title: Locus classicus
definition: The classic or standard source for a view.
